entries.title: Bulls find no-shortcut guy, landing Tiago Splitter as new head coach
entries.summary: <p>It almost felt more pipedream than realistic job description, but Bryson Graham’s expectations were his expectations, and in the world of the Bulls’ new executive vice president of basketball operations there are no shortcuts.</p><p>Tiago Splitter is a no-shortcut guy, and he will now be the organization’s 25<sup>th</sup> head coach, replacing Billy Donovan, a source confirmed on Monday.</p><p>“In terms of what we’re looking for, we’re looking for someone who is smart, we’re looking for someone that can lead, and someone that has a really high character,” Graham said last month in his original requests of what he would be looking for to fill that coaching vacancy. “We also want someone who when I say smart, they’re good on both sides of the ball. A lot of times now you have coaches that lean towards offense and they lean towards defense, and that’s fine, but we’re going to try and find the coach that can coach both sides of the ball and care about both sides of the ball. And then develop these guys, as they are obviously young in their careers.”</p><p>Splitter already has a sample size as an NBA head coach and an impressive one at that. A former NBA Championship player with the Spurs, Splitter became as assistant in Brooklyn back in 2019, eventually working his way to Portland.</p><p>He became the team’s head coach earlier this season, inheriting a complete mess in the wake of former head man Chauncey Billups arrested in connection with an illegal gambling investigation. All Splitter did was refocus a young team to getting in the play-in and beating Phoenix to become a playoff team.</p><p>Portland was flirting with keeping him, but a source told the Sun-Times that his former organization had also been making offers to other coaches in the process.</p>

entries.title: Police searching for man who assaulted, robbed woman at Rainbow Beach Park in South Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Police issued a warning after a woman was sexually assaulted at Rainbow Beach Park in the South Chicago neighborhood on Saturday morning. </p><p>The woman, 44, was jogging in the park near the 3100 block of East 79th Street at 6:15 a.m. when the man attacked her from behind, police said. He then threw her to the ground, sexually assaulted her and took her phone.</p><p>The suspect is described as a Black man in his 30s wearing a blue and gray shirt and jeans, with brown eyes, short black hair, a medium build and standing at about five-foot-eight.</p><p>Anyone with information about the assault can reach CPD at 312-747-8271.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">CRIMINAL SEXUAL ASSAULT & ROBBERY <a href="https://x.com/ChicagoCAPS04?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@ChicagoCAPS04</a> <a href="https://x.com/Area2Detectives?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@Area2Detectives</a> <a href="https://t.co/Fq9ZojkxEa">https://t.co/Fq9ZojkxEa</a> <a href="https://x.com/hashtag/ChicagoPolice?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#ChicagoPolice</a> <a href="https://t.co/eOfGxO9eR2">pic.twitter.com/eOfGxO9eR2</a></p>— Tom Ahern (@TAhern_) <a href="https://x.com/TAhern_/status/2066564119738642883?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">June 15, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: Review: Adamn Killa is the MVP of Summer Smash
entries.summary: <p>We have a saying in Chicago: “We don’t care about celebrities, because we’re the celebrities!”</p><p>Case in point, every time Chicago rapper Adamn Killa would make his way to the viewing area dedicated to dignitaries with his wife and frequent collaborator, Forever Band, over the weekend at Summer Smash, people would scream louder for him than the rappers who were performing, regardless of whether they were among the festival’s anticipated acts like Fetty Wap. As Adamn was leaving another artist’s performance from the pit, fans screamed his name and reached out for handshakes. He took it all in, taking selfies with fans one at a time.</p><p>And that was all before he took to the stage for his own performance on late Sunday afternoon at SeatGeek Stadium in suburban Bridgeview. A lot of this adulation stems from his huge social media notoriety, especially from his “arrest me, daddy” videos. The rapper, who grew up in Chatham and Roseland, would approach an officer and dance in front of them, begging to be arrested (and in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/11/10/chicago-rapper-adamn-killa-tells-cops-to-arrest-me-daddy-getting-arrested-wont-stop-him" target="_blank" ><u>one instance</u></a>, they did arrest him. After they let him go, he went back to making videos). With guilty pleasure viral hits like “Torta Pounder” and “Prada at 13,” his performance on Sunday proved why he’s the real deal who deserves to be viewed as more than an influencer. Seeing the decade of music making on SoundCloud translate to the stage is proof the label is a disservice to him. His fearless, colorful take on rap music made him the MVP of the weekend.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel class="Carousel Enhancement" aria-label="Next"> <svg class="FlickityCustomNavigation-button-icon"><use xlink:href="#icon-right"></use></svg> </button> </div> </div></div> </bsp-carousel> </div> </div><p>An infectious joy was felt throughout his set as young men and women held hands and spun around in a big circle during his set on the SPKRBX stage. Hopping onto the stage with a pink hoodie, bellbottoms made from pink lace and a Hello Kitty bookbag, his performance felt like a call to those who don’t fit into the mainstream to celebrate themselves. Joined by a pink brigade of dancers and his wife, he delivered a medley of his viral hits, including one of earlier songs, “Fall On,” and songs from his album “Influencer” like “Whatever U On” and “Hot.”</p><p>Adamn’s fan service went above and beyond, which is part of why he has such a dedicated audience. At one point, he had the crowd sing “Happy Birthday” to a person named Chance who was celebrating. He even premiered an as-yet-to-be released single dedicated to his wife, “I Like The Way You Walk.” Despite the gloomy weather earlier in the day, the sun came out for Adamn. Hearing all of these songs in the wild, compared to a cellphone, makes his catalog sound so much brighter and grander, as if there was a party all around you.</p><p>The final visual of him, his friends and his entire family all dancing together to “I Can Be” felt like a touching ending to a journey we’ve all seen play out online, the good and the bad. His online presence does not do him justice. Seeing him in real time truly puts his talent in a greater perspective.</p>

entries.title: Brian Urlacher says Bears belong at Soldier Field, tries to tie potential departure to immigration
entries.summary: <p>Brian Urlacher doesn’t like the idea of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> leaving Soldier Field, whether they end up in Hammond, Indiana or Arlington Heights.</p><p>“It doesn’t matter if it’s Indiana or somewhere in Illinois — I can’t picture them leaving Soldier Field,” the Pro Football Hall of Famer told Fox News last week.</p><p>He managed to criticize the state’s immigration policy along the way. He even tried to connect Illinois lawmakers’ inability to reach a property tax funding deal with the Bears to money the state spends as part of its immigration policies.</p><p>"You look at all the money they've given to illegal immigrants and the money they've set aside for that, it's like $2.5, $3 billion that they've spent on the illegal immigrants,” Urlacher claimed. “That money could be for the Bears, could be trying to keep them, not for the Bears, but trying to keep their stadium in town, instead of keeping people that aren't supposed to be in our country here.”</p><p>Urlacher blamed Gov. JB Pritzker and Illinois legislators, saying that “you do what you have to do to keep the Bears there.” Earlier this month, the Bears said they planned to press forward with a proposed site <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/06/12/chicago-bears-soldier-field-hammond-indiana-arlington-heights-stadium-nfl" target="_blank" >in Hammond, Indiana</a>, though they vowed to continue talking to Illinois politicians. Pritzker has said he'd be willing to call a special session if politicians can find momentum on a property tax deal for the Bears. Otherwise, the legislature won't meet in Springfield until November.</p><p>The former linebacker acknowledged that Soldier Field was “already off the table” this year, pointing to Arlington Heights as a valid option. The Bears have said that the 326-acre former Arlington International Racecourse site they own is the only choice they're considering. inside Cook County.</p><p>"They have the land bought already," Urlacher said. "Find a way to keep them there, and they have — they just don’t care."<br></p>

entries.title: Summer Smash 2026: Atlanta-Chicago connection takes center stage
entries.summary: <p>Black Atlanta and Black Chicago are cultural kindred spirits. Both cities have their own histories of unapologetically Black music. Waka Flocka Flame (who performed on Saturday) influenced drill music. Rappers Shawnna and Da Brat became rap superstars through Atlanta record labels. There are even locations of Harold’s Chicken in Atlanta, and both have Black mayors. So it was fitting for Sunday to have a lineup centered on Atlanta rappers Lil Baby and Playboi Carti, while featuring Chicago rappers shaped by Atlanta trap and rage music.</p><p>Dometi Pongo, award-winning journalist and host of <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL7l6WCB1qmAreuecVyuExbdcP-bkPzbdi" target="_blank" ><u>Chess Not Checkers</u></a>, says Chicagoans have been buying into Atlanta’s aesthetic for years. Like many residents, Chicago rappers like Lil Durk would move to Atlanta for a new start but still have that deep-rooted Black culture on every level, like in Chicago.</p><p>“A lot of our favorite rappers relocated to Atlanta, so you see a cross-pollination of culture. And when you go to Atlanta as a Chicagoan, there’s a kindred energy and a kindred relationship. Not only is it a musical influence, but it’s also a cultural influence. Chicago and Atlanta are — I wouldn’t say sister cities, but they’re cities that are in conversation with one another,” said Pongo.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div started rather chilly and wet in the aftermath of a storm that led to SeatGeek Stadium’s grounds being very muddy. The gray skies and slippery terrain made for a rough beginning, but South Suburbanite Thirteendegrees set the tone early at Lenny’s Tent. He was followed by the Chi-lanta hybrid <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/06/12/chicago-born-rapper-raq-baby-summer-smash-debut" >Raq Baby</a>, who brought his mom/manager Toyette Hall on stage to turn up with him and his friends.</p><p>Atlanta was well represented beyond its lineups. Blink, and you would have missed 2025’s headliner, Young Thug, walking around the festival.</p><p>Chicago’s rap daredevil Famous Dex is another beloved staple of Summer Smash. Known for having some of the most intense performances, he showed on Sunday why he was sorely missed last year. He was signed to Atlanta rapper and former friend/collaborator Rich the Kid’s Rich Forever Records until they fell out in 2017. Despite the stumbles he’s experienced from career lows and drug addiction, he still was greeted with a full crowd yelling every word from his hits like “Japan” and “Drip From My Walk.”</p><p>Making an appearance in 2024 alongside Atlanta drill rapper Baby Kia’s festival performance, Roseland rapper MAF Teeski made a mark during his festival debut on the main stage. Despite being nervous, by his own admission, Teeski held his own. In fact, as I arrived inside the stadium, his voice was so loud and distinct that it could be heard from the parking lot.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> Atlanta after signing with Artist Partner Group. He says that many Chicago rappers either move to Atlanta or Los Angeles after breaking out because, for them, staying no longer makes sense for leveling up their careers. Another is that Los Angeles is too glamorous for him, and his image, compared to Atlanta.</p><p>“We’re in the Midwest and blowing up, this the trenches, who the f--- is going to stay here when we’re signed? I went right to Atlanta based off the simple fact L.A. is too popular. Too many palm trees. Your views will go down if they feel like you made it. They still want to see that gutta s---. I always say Atlanta is a baby Chicago,” said MAF Teeski.</p><p>Atlanta’s own Lil Baby made his return to Summer Smash after his 2021 powerhouse performance. Draped in a Gucci black velour sweatsuit, he came back with a vengeance. The whole arena sang word for word, his jams “Drip Too Hard,” “We Paid” and “Freestyle.” His performance is where the “Chicago meets Atlanta”<br>connections are strongest. That SPKRBX stage was the very same one that his friend and collaborator Lil Durk performed on in 2023 during the same time slot. Many thought Lil Baby should’ve closed out the fest this year but that slot went to Playboi Carti, Summer Smash’s longest-running headliner.</p><p>Since 2019, Playboi Carti has become a staple. Co-founder and SPKRBX head Berto Solorio has maintained a long relationship with the rapper and his Opium Records imprint to the point where they’ve held events beyond the festival. legendary performances at Summer Smash, including in 2019, 2022, 2023 and 2024, when he previewed his album “I AM MUSIC.” This one sits at the bottom of that list.</p><p>He was several minutes late, which cut the set short due to the festival’s strict curfew. He delivered some of his most explosive songs over his career, like “Pop Out,” “R.I.P.” and “Rockstar Made,” but he fell short of meeting the standard he set in previous years.</p><p>Maybe he should sit out next year until he has something new to offer.</p>

entries.title: Enfermeros del Hospital St. Mary en Chicago hacen huelga de un día
entries.summary: <p>De pie en medio de la línea de huelga el jueves por la mañana afuera del Hospital St. Mary of Nazareth, Jesús Hernández sintió que la huelga de un día ya era un éxito apenas una hora después de haber comenzado.</p><p>Hernández formaba parte de seis enfermeros <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/06/03/fired-nurses-voice-concerns-over-working-conditions-st-mary-of-nazareth-hospital-amidst-push-to-unionize-chicago" target="_blank" >despedidos en las últimas semanas</a> justo cuando los enfermeros del hospital en el vecindario de Ukrainian Village se preparaban para llevar a cabo una elección para sindicalizarse con el Comité Nacional de Organización de Enfermeros/National Nurses United. Como un mar de azul y rojo, Hernández vio a enfermeros que no conocía bien, quienes se unieron a la línea de huelga para apoyarlos.</p><p>“No tengo miedo, no me voy a echar para atrás”, dijo Hernández. “Sigo aquí en la lucha porque lo que estamos haciendo aquí es importante, porque a las empresas no les importan los pacientes, no les importa el personal. A nosotros nos preocupan los pacientes porque lidiamos con ellos día tras día”.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-970000" name="module-970000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Los automovilistas que pasaban por Division Street tocaron la bocina al ver a la animada multitud que incluía a unos 200 enfermeros sosteniendo letreros que decían: “No puedes despedir a la solidaridad” y “De huelga por mis pacientes”. Los guardias de seguridad estaban afuera de la entrada principal del hospital y en los estacionamientos, pero la huelga continuó sin incidentes hasta hasta la mañana del viernes.</p><p>La huelga ocurrió menos de una semana antes de que aproximadamente 400 enfermeras de St. Mary voten el 17 de junio sobre la formación de un sindicato. Durante la manifestación, los representantes del sindicato y los enfermeros pidieron al hospital que volviera a admitir a los seis enfermeros despedidos. Prime Healthcare, una gran red nacional de hospitales con fines de lucro, adquirió St. Mary y varios otros hospitales en el área de Chicago el año pasado.</p><p>“Estamos cansados de que Prime elimine puestos, como el de enfermería de admisiones, que ayudan a nuestros pacientes a establecerse y nos dan tiempo para cuidar a todos nuestros pacientes”, dijo la enfermera Daisey Moreno. “Prime está más enfocado en recortar personal y despedir enfermeros que en cuidar a nuestros pacientes… Es hora de reintegrar a nuestros compañeros de trabajo y prepararnos para negociar”.</p><div class="Enhancement" de los empleadores privados, incluidos los hospitales, penalizar a los trabajadores por formar un sindicato, según la Junta Nacional de Relaciones Laborales, una agencia federal independiente que protege el derecho a organizarse.</p><p>Fue la segunda manifestación de la esta semana en apoyo a las enfermeras que buscan sindicalizarse en los hospitales del área de Chicago, parte de una ola más amplia de acciones laborales en el cuidado de la salud en todo el país. En ambas manifestaciones, loas enfermeroas exigieron que los hospitales reintegraranadmitieran a sus compañeros de trabajo que fueron despedidos justo cuando estaban formando sindicatos con grupos laborales separados.</p><p>Un coro de funcionarios electos demócratas se ha unido a la lucha para apoyar a las enfermeras de la región, desde el secretario de Estado de Illinois, Alexi Giannoulias, y el senador estadounidense Bernie Sanders, independiente por VermontI-Vt., hasta la senadora estatal Celina Villanueva, demócrata por D-Chicago.</p><p>El hospital St. Maryanta María y su propietario Prime no dijeron cuántoas enfermeroas trabajaron el jueves, manifestando sóolo en un comunicado que el hospital estaba “totalmente dotado de personal según lo planeado para satisfacer las necesidades de nuestros pacientes y brindar atención segura de alta calidad”.</p><p>“Respetamos el derecho de nuestros empleados a participar en actividades sindicales legales y protegidas, y seguimos comprometidos con discusiones continuas de buena fe con nuestroas enfermeroas”, dijo el hospital.</p><p>Noemí Malavé y su hija Crystal Gonzáales, de 17 años, pasaron por la línea de huelgapiquete después de una terapia física en el hospital. Dijeron que el hospital parecía normal, excepto por la mayor presencia de guardias de seguridad. Les dijeron que debían usar gafetes de visitante, lo cual generalmente no tienen que hacer.</p><p>Malavé, del vecindario Logan Square, dijo que su abuela murió en el hospital y que su madre fue paciente de cáncer allí. Aunque loas enfermeroas dicen que el hospital ha cambiado bajo una nueva dirección, Malavé aseguró que no ha notado nada diferente en la calidad de atención en los últimos años.</p><p>“Loas enfermeroas trabajan muy duro y muchas a diferentes horas”, dijo Malavé. “... Creo que merecen todo lo que están pidiendo.”.</p><p>Pero Moreno, la enfermera, le dijo a la multitud durante la manifestación que notó que Prime recortaba gastos para ahorrar dinero, incluyendo la eliminación de un fondo de caridad que ayudaba a los pacientes a comprar medicinas.</p><p>“Quiero que cada uno de mis pacientes obtenga todo lo que necesitan para recuperarsemejorar”, comentódijo Moreno. “Mi trabajo como enfermera es cuidarlos y abogar por ellos, y por eso quise ser parte de la formación de nuestro sindicato.”.</p><p>Nancy Delgado fue una de loas seis enfermeros que fueron despedidas recientemente del St. Mary anta María después de trabajar como enfermera durante siete años. La madre soltera se preocupa por los ahorros de los que ha tenido que depender desde que perdió su trabajo, pero también quiere dar un ejemplo a su hija al alzar la voz.</p><p>“Quiero mostrarle a mi hija que nuestras voces importan, sin importar dónde estés o quién seas”, dijo Delgado. “Tienes el derecho de alzar tu voz y decir la verdad, especialmente si trabajas en el cuidado de la salud.”.</p><p>La acción sindical aumentada en St. Maryanta María es parte de una ola más grande de <a class="Link" anual</a>.</p><p>Loas enfermeroas de Endeavor suplicaron a sus hospitales que respeten el derecho de loas enfermeroas a sindicalizarse, que dejen de vigilarlosvigilarlasey intimidarloas, y que entries.title: White Sox playing match game in bullpen, even with closer Seranthony Dominguez
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> signed Seranthony Dominguez to be their closer. But they don’t always use him that way.</p><p>In fact, until Sunday, he hadn’t pitched in the ninth inning since May 29, and he hadn’t recorded a save since May 25. That’s a span of seven outings.</p><p>What the Sox are doing more often is seeking the best matchups, whenever they happen to come late in games. A perfect example came in their 2-1 victory over the Braves on Wednesday, in which Dominguez pitched the eighth and Bryan Hudson the ninth for the save.</p><p>That’s because three of the Braves’ top four hitters were lefties and four of their bottom five were righties. When manager Will Venable and his staff prepared their game plan, they decided the right-handed Dominguez would face the bottom of the lineup and the left-handed Hudson would face the top – no matter what inning either occurred.</p><p>“If it had happened that in the eighth inning we were at the top, it was going to be Huddy, and the ninth inning would’ve been Ser,” Venable said.</p><p>It didn’t, and Hudson earned his third save of the season. This is how Venable and pitching coach Zach Bove are using the bullpen, and it’s hard to argue with the results. That’s one reason why you won’t hear Dominguez complaining.</p><p>“I’m just here for the team, trying to be one of the best teammates,” said Dominguez, who earned his 12th save Sunday in a 6-4 victory over the Dodgers. “Whatever they’re doing, it’s working. We got first place, and we’re playing good baseball. At the end of the day, I’m here to pitch when they call my name.”</p><p>“We’ve had a lot of conversations with Seranthony and the rest of the bullpen guys that regardless of the roles or the labels that they might have, we’re going to do what we have to do to get through a game,” said Venable, who has seven pitchers with at least one save, tied for the fourth-most in the majors.</p><p>“What is great about Ser and the rest of the guys is that, while of course Ser wants to close games, and he will continue to close games, he’s understanding that for us to find our path to winning, it might be best for him and for other relievers and for our club to pitch in the eighth.”</p><p>No one on the Sox’ pitching staff has displayed more versatility this season than lefty Sean Newcomb, who has entered games between the second and ninth innings, often throwing multiple innings. On Sunday, he was the second opener behind Hudson — who, along with Grant Taylor, have opened and closed games — throwing 2 ⅓ scoreless innings.</p><p>“It’s what I signed here to do,” Newcomb said, “knowing that it would be more leverage and a little bit more length, depending on what the night called for. There’s a ton of value in coming in tied, one- or two-run game, and holding it there.”</p><p>Newcomb has done that more often than not, allowing only two earned runs in his last 26 innings. Taylor had been on a similar run — generally pitching between the sixth and the ninth — allowing two earned runs in his previous 23 ⅓ innings before giving up two runs in two innings Sunday. Still, his ERA is only 2.21.</p><p>“It’s not only the best matchup, it’s the buy-in from the players, whatever’s going to help the team win,” Bove said. “It’s easy to say that, but to then do that and show that, it’s been awesome.”</p><h3>Saving the day</h3><p>The White Sox have seven pitchers with at least one save, the fourth-most in the majors. entries.title: Explosivo sospechoso rompe ventana de la casa del concejal Byron Sigcho López en Pilsen
entries.summary: <p>Una explosión poco después de la medianoche del sábado en Pilsen destrozó una ventana en la casa del concejal Byron Sigcho López (25.º), pero no se reportaron lesionados.</p><p>Videos e imágenes proporcionadas por la oficina del concejal del distrito 25 muestran a alguien encendiendo un explosivo en el suelo que detona y genera una nube de humo. En el video se pueden oír cristales rompiéndose y una alarma de automóvil.</p><p>La explosión ocurrió a eso de las 12:45 a.m. cerca del oeste de la intersección 21st Street y Damen Avenue, según la oficina de Sigcho López, que también indicó que sus tres hijos estaban dentro de la casa durmiendo en ese momento.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8b0000" name="module-8b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>La Policía de Chicago indicó que se sospecha que el explosivo era un artefacto pirotécnico.</p><p>La oficina de Sigcho López citó videos de vigilancia que muestran a dos hombres en un vehículo SUV acercándose al área. Un hombre se bajó del auto, encendió el explosivo y regresó al vehículo antes de que se marcharan.</p><p>La Unidad de Bombas e Incendios del Departamento de Policía de Chicago (CPD) está investigando, según la oficina del concejal. entries.title: Man gunned down in West Garfield Park
entries.summary: <p>Police are looking for the assailant responsible for fatally shooting a 32-year-old man Monday afternoon in the West Garfield Park neighborhood. </p><p>The unidentified man was killed about 12:45 p.m. in the 3900 block of West Flournoy Street, police said. </p><p>He suffered multiple gunshot wounds and was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital, where he was pronounced dead, according to police. </p><p>No arrests were reported. </p><p>Area 4 detectives are investigating. </p>

entries.title: Man screamed racial slur at 9-year-old boy, pushed him off bike in Naperville, police say
entries.summary: <p>A Plainfield man was released with a GPS monitor after being charged with a hate crime for allegedly yelling a racial slur at a 9-year-old boy, pushing him and throwing his bike in Naperville over the weekend. </p><p>Jeffrey Feigenbaum, 29, of the 15800 block of Cove Circle, appeared in court Sunday, charged with with two counts of hate crime and one count each of misdemeanor battery and disorderly conduct, according to the DuPage County state’s attorney’s office.</p><p>Naperville officers responded Saturday in the 1400 block of West Jefferson Avenue for a report of a white adult male pushing a Black child and using a racial slur, authorities said.</p><p>Prosecutors said the boy and some friends had been building a fort down the street when a girl, later identified as Feigenbaum’s girlfriend’s daughter, allegedly damaged the fort.</p><p>When the boy went to the girl’s home on West Jefferson Avenue and knocked on the door, Feigenbaum allegedly left the home, yelled a racial slur at the boy, pushed him and threw his bike as he ran away, prosecutors said.</p><p>The court denied the state’s motion to detain Feigenbaum during his Sunday hearing, and he was released with conditions, including that he be fitted with a GPS monitor, stay at least 5,000 feet away from the boy, his home and his school, and surrender all firearms and other weapons to Naperville police.</p><p>“The allegations against Mr. Feigenbaum are very disturbing,” DuPage County State’s Attorney Robert Berlin said in a statement. “Hate crimes have no place in a civilized society. DuPage County is comprised of dozens of extremely welcoming and diverse communities, and the type of behavior alleged in this case will not be tolerated.”</p><p>A statement released from Naperville police also condemned the suspect's alleged actions.</p><p>“Every person in our community has the right to live free from intimidation, violence, and hate,” Naperville Chief of Police Jason Arres said in a statement. “Conduct involving threats, physical aggression and racial slurs directed at a child is completely unacceptable and stands in direct opposition to the values we expect and uphold in Naperville.”</p><p>Feigenbaum is due back in court July 13. <br></p>

entries.title: Shootings increased near Chicago’s closed schools that sat empty, study finds
entries.summary: <p>As Chicago officials prepared to close 50 schools in 2013, the most at one time in American history, neighbors warned that the ramifications would go beyond worse academic outcomes for students. They worried the vacant buildings left behind would hurt their communities.</p><p>Thirteen years later, a new study from the University of Chicago and Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health has found that the closings, in fact, led to a 10% increase in gun violence in the areas surrounding the vacant closed schools compared to neighborhoods with similar demographics where schools didn’t close.</p><p>The researchers found no statistically significant increase in shootings in communities where closed schools were repurposed, which city officials promised would happen.</p><p>"We found that school closure and subsequent building vacancy were associated with significant increases in firearm violence in affected neighborhoods, and that this association appeared to be partially mitigated by subsequent school buildings re-use,” the authors wrote in the study, <a class="Link" href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0277953626005046?via%3Dihub" target="_blank" ><u>published in the journal Social Science & Medicine</u></a>.</p><p>The new research adds to a pile of evidence that the closures, at best, didn’t produce transformative outcomes for students and communities, and at worst, they hurt kids and neighborhoods.</p><p>“We were interested in thinking about [closed] schools not just as a vacant lot, because they represent so much more in a community,” said Thomas Statchen, a UChicago medical student and lead author of the study. They’re public spaces and “sites of other community events, activities, playgrounds — all these things that are lost alongside a school,” he said.</p><p>A 2023 Chicago Sun-Times and WBEZ series, “<a class="Link" href="https://graphics.suntimes.com/education/2023/chicagos-50-closed-schools/" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago’s 50 Closed Schools</u></a>,” found a slew of broken promises by leaders in the decade after the closings: Many buildings <a class="Link" href="https://graphics.suntimes.com/education/2023/chicagos-50-closed-schools/buildings/" target="_blank" ><u>were not repurposed</u></a>, despite vows by city officials to repurpose them as community centers, housing or other projects, with only actually 20 back in use. <a class="Link" href="https://graphics.suntimes.com/education/2023/chicagos-50-closed-schools/kids/" target="_blank" ><u>Academic outcomes didn’t improve</u></a> for the students who left the closed schools. And <a class="Link" href="https://graphics.suntimes.com/education/2023/chicagos-50-closed-schools/welcoming-schools/" target="_blank" ><u>increased funding didn’t last</u></a> at the schools that absorbed them.</p><p>Selling the vacant schools has proven difficult because of a lack of buyer interest and deteriorating building conditions. Some sales and projects have fallen through and the successful ones can take several years. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/01/29/closed-cps-schools-armstrong-paderewski-athletic-center-affordable-housing" target="_blank" ><u>CPS stepped up its efforts late last year</u></a> and identified buyers for five vacant schools. But in all, 14 empty buildings were still publicly owned in January.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a is still trying to sell.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Brian Rich/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The new research from UChicago and Johns Hopkins adds more pressure on public officials to solve longstanding budget challenges, particularly at schools that have lost significant enrollment over the past two decades, without closing more schools — or to have plans in place for vacant buildings.</p><p>Whether to close or consolidate schools is on the minds of some voters and candidates as Chicago gears up to choose members of its first fully elected school board this fall. Nearly 900 CPS parents and residents responded to a <a class="Link" href="https://airtable.com/appu9nu8BNBrotoOR/pagRg1TV9UI2TfPGd/form" target="_blank" ><u>WBEZ/Sun-Times questionnaire</u></a> this spring with concerns and questions about the school system. Low-enrollment and under-utilized schools — and their effect on CPS’ budget — was a top issue.</p><p>CPS is grappling with widespread budget cuts for a second year as it faces a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/05/13/as-cps-cuts-staff-to-plug-deficit-educator-unions-and-school-board-members-press-for-more-state-funding" target="_blank" ><u>projected $732 million deficit</u></a> for the upcoming school year. Officials have said they want to cut spending in ways that don’t affect classrooms and offerings in schools, but that appears difficult.</p><p>The study by Statchen and five co-authors analyzed police crime data from 2010 to 2019 and found that areas surrounding vacant schools, mostly on the South and West sides, saw about a 10% increase in shootings after the 2013 closings compared to areas with similar racial demographics and poverty rates where schools remained open. The communities that had an uptick in gun violence also experienced increases in weapons violations and firearm-related assaults and batteries.</p><p>The researchers said the findings suggest that long-term vacancy of closed schools is “potentially a key factor contributing to increased firearm violence.”</p><p>“You really get to know people who live by you because you go to school with them,” said study co-author Elizabeth Tung, an associate professor of medicine at UChicago. “It’s like it’s not just evicting a family, you’re evicting an entire neighborhood, or an entire community, from their school.”</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson fought school closings when he was an organizer with the Chicago Teachers Union before his election. As mayor, he has called on Illinois lawmakers to spend more on education statewide to help CPS and other school systems struggling after pandemic relief funding ran out, highlighting funding shortages. If the city’s elected school board examines whether to close schools, findings from the UChicago study and the Sun-Times/WBEZ series suggest leaders should tread lightly. A moratorium on school closings in Chicago expires next year.</p><p>“Multiple U.S. cities are once again considering significant school closures,” the researchers wrote. “While the decision to close a school is extremely complex and politically-charged, this study indicates that there may be broad consequences — including potential increases in firearm violence — if schools are vacated without concomitant plans for community investment and development.”</p><p><b><i>Contributing:</i></b><i> Al Keefe</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://graphics.suntimes.com/education/2023/chicagos-50-closed-schools/" >Chicago closed 50 public schools 10 years ago. Did the city keep its promises?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Chicago's top federal prosecutor 'weighing' options after appeals court formally undoes ComEd convictions
entries.summary: <p>The question of whether to retry two former ComEd officials caught up in a massive corruption investigation officially landed in the lap of U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros on Monday, when Chicago’s federal appeals court released a 16-page opinion<b> </b>formally<b> </b>wiping out their convictions.</p><p>Two months have passed since the 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/comed-bribery-trial/2026/04/14/madigan-bribery-comed-conspiracy-bribery-chicago-crime-pramaggiore-mcclain" target="_blank" >ordered the release</a> from prison of former ComEd CEO Anne<b> </b>Pramaggiore and<b> </b>longtime<b> </b>ComEd<b> </b>lobbyist<b> </b>Michael<b> </b>McClain. That means the opinion from a three-judge panel came as no surprise.</p><p>But Boutros refrained from commenting on his plans for Pramaggiore and McClain until after he had a chance to read the appeals court’s official reasoning. The judges' final opinion found the 2023<b> </b>conviction of Pramaggiore<b> </b>and McClain legally problematic, but it also ended with a word of caution.</p><p>“Do not misread our opinion,” it said. “We are not suggesting that Pramaggiore and McClain are innocent, only that their convictions were flawed and that they have a right to see their sentences vacated.”</p><p>U.S. District Judge Manish<b> </b>Shah<b> </b>sentenced <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-corruption-trials/2025/07/21/former-comed-ceo-gets-2-year-prison-sentence" target="_blank" >Pramaggiore</a><b> </b>and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-corruption-trials/2025/07/24/madigans-political-fixer-gets-2-year-prison-sentence" target="_blank" >McClain</a> in 2025 to two years in prison for their role in a lengthy conspiracy to illegally sway former Illinois House Speaker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/madigan-trial-news" target="_blank" >Michael J. Madigan</a>. The former speaker was convicted separately and is still in prison.</p><p>In a statement Monday, Boutros called the appeals court’s ruling “well-reasoned and thoughtful.” He also noted that it found “significant and compelling evidence”<b> </b>had been presented at trial.</p><p>“Because the Seventh Circuit has stated that the government is ‘entitled to retry’ both defendants ‘at its discretion,’ we are weighing our options and will advise the District Court of our decision at the appropriate time,” Boutros said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros will have to decide whether to retry Anne Pramaggiore and Michael McClain in federal court.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The appeals court said it could not be sure that jurors convicted Pramaggiore and McClain on a legal basis that remains valid after<b> </b>a 2024<b> </b>U.S. Supreme Court ruling, though.</p><p>Judge<b> </b>Thomas<b> </b>Kirsch<b> </b>wrote Monday’s opinion, in which he was joined by Judges<b> </b>David<b> </b>Hamilton<b> </b>and<b> </b>Joshua<b> </b>Kolar. Kirsch was appointed by President Donald Trump, Hamilton by President Barack Obama and Kolar by President Joe Biden.</p><p>The question of whether to take McClain and Pramaggiore to trial again comes at a particularly fraught time for Boutros. His office has spent the last three weeks trying to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/12/broadview-six-boutros-chicago-abughazaleh-justice-department-doj" target="_blank" >contain fallout</a> after allegations of prosecutorial misconduct <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >led to the collapse of a case</a> it brought against a group of Operation Midway Blitz protesters known as the “Broadview Six.”</p><p>Last week, his office also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/11/broadview-six-grand-jury-misconduct-federal-prosecutors-drop-charges-loretto-hospital-covid-fraud" target="_blank" >dropped charges</a> against two others in a fraud case tied to Loretto Hospital after a judge <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/10/hearing-in-loretto-hospital-case-could-address-claims-of-prosecutors-misconduct-if-feds-dont-drop-it" target="_blank" >threatened to hold an evidentiary hearing</a> over similar alleged misconduct by the same prosecutor involved in the “Broadview Six” case.</p><p>Another judge said Boutros and his leadership team had created a “credibility crisis.”</p><p>Two of the four prosecutors who tried Pramaggiore and McClain in 2023 have left the U.S. attorney’s office. And McClain and Pramaggiore have each served roughly three months behind bars.</p><p>They were convicted on one count of conspiracy, as well as four bribery counts and four counts of falsifying ComEd’s books and records.</p><p>Shortly before the pair could be sentenced, the Supreme Court picked up <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-corruption-trials/2024/06/26/supreme-court-snyder-ruling-madigan-corruption" target="_blank" >a corruption case from Northwest Indiana</a> that revolved around the same bribery law used to prosecute Pramaggiore and McClain.</p><p>In June 2024,<b> </b>the high court found<b> </b>that the law does not criminalize after-the-fact rewards known as "gratuities." Nine months later, Shah <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/comed-bribery-trial/2025/03/03/comed-bribery-case-four-counts-tossed-foreign-corrupt-practices-act" target="_blank" >threw out the bribery convictions</a> against Pramaggiore and McClain but left the remaining convictions intact.</p><p>Their remaining conspiracy conviction featured multiple so-called “objects,”<b> </b>including some that were invalidated by the Supreme Court’s ruling. The appeals court said Monday<b> </b>it could not be sure that jurors rested their conviction on a theory that remains valid.</p><p>“Pramaggiore and McClain have the right to a jury verdict, and we do not know what the jury did,” the panel concluded.</p><p>Because Madigan went to trial after the Supreme Court’s ruling, the judge and lawyers in his case had the benefit of the high court’s guidance. The appeals court upheld Madigan’s conviction<b> </b>in April, and he continues to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/06/13/mike-madigan-sentencing-hearing" target="_blank" >serve a<b> </b>7 ½-year prison sentence</a> in West Virginia.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/comed-bribery-trial/2026/04/14/madigan-bribery-comed-conspiracy-bribery-chicago-crime-pramaggiore-mcclain" target="_blank" >Ex-ComEd CEO, Madigan ally to be freed from prison as appeals court calls for new trial in conspiracy case</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/madigan-trial-news/2026/04/06/madigan-comed-corruption-supreme-appelate-court" target="_blank" >Madigan, ex-ComEd defendants assembled a high-powered legal team for appeals court arguments this month</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/12/broadview-six-boutros-chicago-abughazaleh-justice-department-doj" target="_blank" >‘Is Mr. Boutros here?’ Judge drops fraud charges, calls out U.S. attorney as ‘Broadview 6’ fallout grows</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/99/fa/3c6399554c89994771324a7d9ddf/pramaggioremcclain7th.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: Oak Park police investigating antisemitic vandalism
entries.summary: <p>Oak Park police are investigating a report of antisemitic vandalism, the department announced.</p><p>The incident was reported Wednesday in the 300 block of Home Avenue, and detectives have canvassed the area and reviewed security footage, according to a release from Oak Park police. It's currently being investigated as criminal damage to property, but hate crime charges could be filed, spokesperson Dan Yopchick said.</p><p>"Acts of antisemitism have no place in Oak Park," Village President Vicki Scaman said in a statement. "Our village prides itself on being a welcoming, diverse community and incidents like this one are deeply painful, not just for those directly affected, but for our entire Jewish community and all residents who value inclusion."</p><p>Oak Park police are working with other departments in the area to identify any possible trends or patterns of similar incidents.</p><p>Anyone with information can contact Oak Park police at 708.386.3800 or police@oak-park.us. </p>

entries.title: Queen of Martyrs school in Evergreen Park closing due to declining enrollment
entries.summary: <p>Queen of Martyrs School in south suburban Evergreen Park will not reopen for the upcoming school year, the Archdiocese of Chicago announced Monday.</p><p>The school's enrollment has declined considerably, partly due to allegations earlier this year that a former substitute teacher inappropriately touched a second grader, leaving the school unable to operate, superintendent of schools Greg Richmond said in a statement posted on the school's Facebook page.</p><p>"Events earlier this year, including concerns related to a personnel matter, shook the trust of some families and contributed to their decision to leave," Richmond said. "That reality is painful to acknowledge. At the same time, the school's challenges did not begin this year and are not the result of a single event."</p><p>The family of a second grade boy sued Brett J. Smith, a substitute teacher who was fired by the archdiocese, in January, alleging he groomed and touched their child inappropriately. The lawsuit also alleged church officials were aware of Smith's past sexual abuse allegations and failed to disclose them to parents.</p><p>Enrollment at the school has been declining over the past decade, falling from 325 students in 2016 to a projected 140 students for next school year.</p><p>"The decline in next year's enrollment would create an under-resourced school, unable to provide the quality education students need and deserve," Richmond said. "Fewer students means fewer resources to provide the modern, rigorous and holistic education that parents expect from a Catholic school."</p><p>The school would operate at a deficit of more than $400,000 next year, according to projections, Richmond said in the statement. </p><p>The archdiocese will help families at the school consider other Catholic school options for the fall.</p><p>"Queen of Martyrs has been a place where children have been known, loved, taught and formed in faith," Richmond said. "That legacy will not be forgotten."<br></p>
entries.author: Mary Norkol

entries.title: Skylar Diggins knows small mistakes will cost Sky against Liberty
entries.summary: <p>If there’s one thing that sticks out to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> point guard Skylar Diggins about the Liberty — aside from their sheer amount of talent — it’s their length.</p><p>The Liberty’s frontcourt features Breanna Stewart (6-4), Jonquel Jones (6-6) and Satou Sabally (6-4), all of whom are forces inside. On the perimeter, Leonie Fiebich (6-4) and Pauline Astier (5-11) take away passing lanes and make every shot difficult.</p><p>‘‘That’s the theme of what I see,’’ Diggins told the Sun-Times after practice Sunday. ‘‘Deflections, steals, blocked shots.’’</p><p>The Liberty — who will visit Wednesday — have the third-best record, second-best defense and fourth-best rebounding mark in the WNBA. They’ve done it while adjusting to a new coach and rarely playing at full strength.</p><p>Sabally still is coming off the bench as she works her way back from an extended recovery from a concussion. All-Star guard Sabrina Ionescu recently returned after missing seven games with back soreness.</p><p>Coach Chris DeMarco, a longtime Warriors assistant, took over after the Liberty fired Sandy Brondello, who led them to the 2024 title.</p><p>The injuries and new system meant the Liberty didn’t immediately meld into championship form, even though many preseason power rankings put them at the top of the league. They dropped a few surprising games early, including two to the expansion Fire, but have won seven in a row since.</p><p>‘‘They’re clicking right now,’’ Sky coach Tyler Marsh said Monday. ‘‘They’re getting their rhythm back. Having Sabrina back in the lineup helps them. They’re a championship-caliber team, and we always knew that coming into it. It was just a matter of time before they got used to a new system and new coaching staff.’’</p><p>The Liberty will test the Sky where they’re weakest. The Sky rank last in the league in rebounding, too often failing to finish otherwise-solid defensive possessions. They also have struggled to get their bigs, Kamilla Cardoso and Azura Stevens, out to contest opposing post players on the perimeter.</p><p>The Liberty can punish them on both fronts. Sabally and Jones each are shooting around 40% from three-point range.</p><p>Given the Liberty’s shooting, length and star power, Marsh said applying pressure is key.</p><p>‘‘We can’t afford to sit back and let them run action freely,’’ he said. ‘‘We’ve got to be disruptive and allow them to feel our presence.’’</p><p>Ball pressure has helped keep the Sky in games when <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/06/09/tyler-marsh-has-taken-the-blame-for-the-skys-offense-but-its-actually-complicated" target="_blank" >their offense waffles</a>. But even that hasn’t been consistent, especially when <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/06/10/call-her-energizer-bunny-or-team-papi-the-sky-go-as-natasha-cloud-goes" target="_blank" >their best perimeter defender</a>, Natasha Cloud, gets into foul trouble. Cloud fouled out of an overtime loss last week to the Fever.</p><p>The Sky have lost seven of their last eight games and still haven’t figured out whom they are after losing leading scorer Rickea Jackson to a torn ACL. They also remain without two key pieces in Courtney Vandersloot and DiJonai Carrington.</p><p>This week, which features difficult matchups against the Liberty and Wings, will test whether the Sky’s recent fight can stay consistent. They have built some momentum in the last two games, taking two playoff teams down to the wire.</p><p>‘‘I guess if we’re talkin’ about moral victories, we played harder,’’ Diggins said Sunday of the last two games. ‘‘Showed a lot of grit in those games. We know that can be our identity. I know we spoke early about wanting to have that type of identity. We have kind of fallen short.’’</p><p>In the end, grit is only a starting point. Diggins said she wants the Sky to prove they can finish and commit to fixing the details that keep costing them, especially on the glass.</p><p>Toward the end of practice Monday, Diggins stopped the session to make sure the Sky were executing their rebounding scheme on free throws, too. She called it a tedious detail but wanted to make sure it sank in.</p><p>The message was clear: We’re already struggling with this. Let’s not make it worse with small mistakes.</p><p>Otherwise, the Liberty will make them pay.</p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: Illinois lawmakers eye nation's first ban on AI-powered smart glasses for drivers
entries.summary: <p>Eyes on the road — and off your fancy glasses.</p><p>That’s the order from Illinois lawmakers who advanced a bill late in their spring session to bar drivers from wearing smart glasses powered by artificial intelligence.</p><p>The high-tech specs that have grown in popularity allow users to watch and record videos, send messages and scroll through plenty of the other minutiae that too many drivers are already distracting themselves with on their cellphones, according to Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias.</p><p>“Distracted driving is the drunk driving of our generation,” said Giannoulias, who championed the bill that received unanimous support in the Illinois General Assembly. “AI glasses shouldn’t become the next excuse for taking your attention off the road.”</p><p>The bill awaits Gov. JB Pritzker’s signature to make Illinois the first state to ban drivers from wearing smart glasses.</p><p>The proposed legislation specifically adds “artificial intelligence smart glasses” to the list of electronic communication devices already barred from use behind the wheel under state law.</p><p>That includes phones, hand-held personal digital assistants, tablets and computers that aren’t integrated into vehicles. Existing law includes some exemptions for hands-free, voice-operated use, which wouldn’t apply for smart glasses.</p><p>It’s not clear if smart glasses have been involved in more crashes in recent years, but anecdotally, they’re becoming more of an issue for Illinois police departments and DMVs, according to Giannoulias.</p><p>“We began seeing people wearing these smart glasses while taking their written exams and behind-the-wheel road tests,” he said. “It raised legitimate concerns about cheating and other challenges they can pose. Distracted driving is an epidemic, and these pose the same risks as other electronic devices.”</p><p>More than 3,200 people were killed and 315,000 injured in crashes involving distracted drivers nationwide in 2024, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/IZkevLcZjO4?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="General Assembly Passes Giannoulias Measure Targeting Emerging Distracted Driving Threats from AI"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p></p>

entries.title: Los White Sox dicen que ya no se deben sorprender: están ganando
entries.summary: <p>Si pensabas que los líderes de la división, los Braves y los Dodgers, iban a poner a los White Sox en su lugar antes de que visitaran el Rate Field, no estabas solo. Un récord de 0.500 como mucho en seis juegos en casa podría haberse visto como una victoria moral, con lecciones aprendidas a los pies de los mejores del béisbol.</p><p>Pero después de que los Sox vencieron a los Dodgers 6-4 el domingo para terminar 4-1 en la homestand abreviada, los únicos que están aprendiendo lecciones son los incrédulos. Los Sox siguen marcando casillas para ser considerados un serio contendiente para los playoffs y tienen otra oportunidad esta semana contra otro equipo líder, los Yankees.</p><p>“Creo que deberían dejar de pensar en esto como una sorpresa sólo porque estamos ganando de manera constante y en cada juego”, dijo el parador en corto Colson Montgomery, quien conectó uno de los tres jonrones en una sexta entrada de seis carreras. “No importa qué equipo sea, vamos a salir a jugar nuestro béisbol. Creo que esos días ya pasaron”.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-9f0000" name="module-9f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>En estos días, los Sox están ganando de todas las maneras posibles. El domingo, lo hicieron con no uno sino dos relevistas antes de que el abridor habitual Erick Fedde asumiera el mando en la cuarta entrada. Podrías llamarlo un juego de relevistas porque las 2⅔ entradas de Fedde fueron las más largas entre los cinco lanzadores.</p><p>Fedde, quien vivió gran parte de la miseria de los Sox en 2024 en su camino hacia su récord de 121 derrotas en Grandes Ligas, dijo que pensaba que las cosas eran diferentes con este equipo de los Sox en el entrenamiento de primavera.</p><p>“Miramos a nuestro alrededor y pensamos, ‘Este es un equipo que tiene mucho talento’”, comentó. “Obviamente, salir y demostrarlo es algo completamente diferente, pero los muchachos aquí no están sorprendidos. Y creo que la forma en que hemos estado jugando contra esta serie de oponentes de calidad, supongo que estamos poniendo a la liga un poco más en aviso”.</p><p>Y continúan haciéndolo sin su máximo bateador de jonrones, Munetaka Murakami. Aún más sorprendente, están anotando más carreras sin él. Antes de que Murakami dejara el juego el 29 de mayo con una lesión en el tendón de los isquiotibiales, los Sox tenían un promedio de 4.7 carreras por juego. En los 14 juegos que han perdido, tienen un promedio 5.3.</p><p>Sam Antonacci y Chase Meidroth también conectaron cuadrangulares en la sexta. El de Antonacci abrió la entrada y fue el primero que pasó por encima del muro. Al igual que el de Montgomery, el de Meidroth fue un jonrón de dos carreras. La otra carrera vino de un doble de Andrew Benintendi.</p><p>Los primeros seis bateadores en la entrada llegaron a base, de los cuales los tres primeros tuvieron una tercera oportunidad contra el abridor de los Dodgers, Emmet Sheehan, quien estaba lanzando bien, limitando a los Sox a un hit y ponchando a ocho en cinco entradas. Montgomery dijo que eso marcó la diferencia.</p><p>“[Nuestros entrenadores] seguían diciéndonos que nos mantuviéramos con nuestro plan de juego, mantuviéramos nuestro enfoque, y seguimos peleando en los turnos al bate”, dijo. “Porque [Sheehan] estaba lanzando bien. Solo teníamos el sentido de que si nos manteníamos así, íbamos a lograrlo contra él”.</p><p>La victoria no llegó sin un palpitante momento en el noveno, cuando el cerrador Seranthony Domínguez trajo al representante de la carrera de la ventaja a la caja de bateo. Con corredores en primera y tercera y dos outs, Domínguez ponchó a Freddie Freeman para finalizar el juego.</p><p>“Creo que cada victoria en la serie, estos muchachos siguen ganando confianza, ciertamente contra un buen equipo”, dijo el mánager Will Venable. “Es importante; importa asegurar esa victoria hoy. Pero estos muchachos no creo que necesiten necesariamente ese tipo de oponente para ganar confianza. Es una victoria en la serie, y eso es lo más importante”.</p><p>Ahora es el turno de Nueva York, donde los Sox tienen programado enfrentar a Gerrit Cole el martes y al exzurdo de los Sox, Carlos Rodón, el miércoles. Los Yankees son otra casilla que los Sox deben marcar, aunque no contarán con el bateador de poder lesionado Aaron Judge.</p><p>“Sabemos que tenemos otro buen desafío aquí en Nueva York”, dijo Venable. “Así que tenemos que disfrutar de esta victoria en un vuelo feliz para estos muchachos, tendremos un día libre y luego [volveremos] a los negocios”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Mayor Johnson's social media tax generating windfall of revenue amid legal challenge
entries.summary: <p>Chicago is on pace to collect $49.2 million during the first year of Mayor Brandon Johnson’s groundbreaking<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/10/21/brandon-johnson-social-media-tax-chicago-budget" > tax on social media </a>companies — nearly 60% above the city’s original estimate — raising the stakes for a court challenge by Big Tech.</p><p>The City Council’s Finance Committee was informed of the potential windfall Monday as it refined the definition of the tax in an apparent attempt to strengthen the city’s case and better coincide with the state’s version of the tax.</p><p>The social media tax — at a rate of 50 cents per user after the first 100,000 users — was expected to raise $31 million during all of 2026.</p><p>But Johnson’s policy chief, Jung Yoon, told the Finance Committee that the city collected $16.4 million during the first four months alone from the 10 social media companies to which the levy has applied. They are: Meta, owner of Instagram, Facebook and Threads; YouTube; X; Snap; TikTok; LinkedIn; Reddit; Twitch; Pinterest; and NextDoor.</p><p>At that rate, the first-year take would be $49.2 million, 58.7% higher than anticipated.</p><p>“I’m surprised that it’s doing so well,” Finance Chair Pat Dowell (3rd) told the Sun-Times. “This is like the first time we’re ever seeing a tax like this. I don’t think anybody really knew what it could generate. And it is performing well above expectations. … That bodes well for the city.”</p><p>A coalition of the world’s largest tech companies is seeking to overturn the tax on grounds that the first-of-its-kind per-user levy tramples over the First Amendment rights of major corporations that contend they’re part of the free press.</p><p>The Circuit Court lawsuit was filed in mid-March by the tech trade group NetChoice and is in the early stages of discovery, the Finance Committee was told.</p><p>Ald. Nicole Lee (11th) said the apparent windfall from the social media tax could leave the city with a giant hole when it comes to bankrolling future mental health programs.</p><p>“It is a gamble. The administration has to understand that,” Lee said. “My fear is a net loss on this one if we don’t succeed in winning this lawsuit. … I hope we don’t lose it. But I don’t think it’s an unfounded fear.”</p><p>Former Finance Chair Scott Waguespack (32nd) said the social media tax is "easy to collect," but it will be "harder to give the money back."</p><p>“We could have a big hole a year after, or two years after, when the courts potentially say you don’t have standing, you lose the case. Then we have to go find … what could be $100 million-plus," Waguespack said.</p><p></p><p></p><p>For now, the higher-than-expected revenues are being held in escrow — what Dowell calls a “lockbox” — pending the outcome of the legal challenge. In the meantime, those social programs are being bankrolled by the city’s corporate fund.</p><p>“It just means we can’t expand these programs” if we lose the legal challenge, Dowell said.</p><p>In an apparent attempt to strengthen the city’s case and match legal definitions included in the state’s version of the social media tax, the Finance Committee approved Johnson’s plan to “clarify definitions” in the city tax as well as the law’s “original intent.”</p><p>One of the refined definitions makes it clear that “social media means a website, platform or other application where users provide the content.”</p><p>“This is in contrast to platforms, websites or applications where the content is created or selected for inclusion by those who maintain the website platform and not the users themselves. So, think about like the Washington Post or other [news] websites like that,” Yung told the Finance Committee.</p><p>“It removes from the definition of social media any reference to bona fide news websites, applications or internet platforms," Yung said, adding "that was not necessary in inclusion of the definition because those websites do not fall under the definition of social media under the law.”</p><p>Yet another change would clarify which uses count toward the tax.</p><p>“It clarifies that it’s applicable where there is a use by a Chicago consumer during a calendar month, even if the platform had previously collected data on that consumer, they have to be actively using it for that month to count toward the tax,” Yoon said.</p><p>Dowell called the changes "a common sense vote," adding, “You have to be a social media company. We shouldn’t be taxing the Tribune … or Sun-Times.”</p><p>In other City Council news, a subject matter hearing on the sale of Chicago parking meters to a New York investment firm was postponed until June 25 to give Finance Committee members time to review more than 700 pages of documents provided by the New York firm, Stonepeak Partners, on Friday evening. Dowell credited Stonepeak with being "very forthright with information" that her colleagues needed more time to review.</p>
